Make sure you use Opus sub-agents to do all your work. They are effectively free. Parallelize them as much as possible. Have Fable and Sol, and Opus agents review any production code work or plans. There are architect agents for plan reviewing and code review agents for code reviewing. Save your context Any finished agents remove them to keep statusbar clean

the nightly build failed - diagnose why and tell me plain english only

Read-only: never edits code. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- architect-opus: Designs implementation architectures: analyzes existing codebase patterns, then delivers a blueprint — files to create/modify, component design, data flow, build sequence, risks, alternatives. Read-only: never edits code. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- architect-sol: Designs implementation architectures: analyzes existing codebase patterns, then delivers a blueprint — files to create/modify, component design, data flow, build sequence, risks, alternatives. Read-only: never edits code. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- code-reviewer-fable: Adversarial code review of diffs/commits/PRs: correctness, security, data integrity, conventions. Verifies each finding before reporting, ranks BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR with file:line and concrete failure scenario. Read-only: never fixes. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-reviewer-opus: Adversarial code review of diffs/commits/PRs: correctness, security, data integrity, conventions. Verifies each finding before reporting, ranks BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR with file:line and concrete failure scenario. Read-only: never fixes. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-reviewer-sol: Adversarial code review of diffs/commits/PRs: correctness, security, data integrity, conventions. Verifies each finding before reporting, ranks BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR with file:line and concrete failure scenario. Read-only: never fixes. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- project-structure-validator: Validates project structure against co-location and architecture patterns defined in AGENTS.md (Tools: All tools)

- sol: General-purpose subagent running on Codex GPT-5.6 Sol via the claude-all gateway. Use for heavy implementation, deep debugging, second-opinion reviews, or any Task the orchestrator wants executed by GPT-5.6 Sol instead of a Claude model. Accepts any prompt a general-purpose agent would. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- understand-anything:architecture-analyzer: Analyzes a codebase's file structure, summaries, and import relationships to identify
logical architectural layers and assign every file to exactly one layer. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:article-analyzer: Analyzes markdown files using pre-parsed structural data and LLM inference to extract knowledge graph nodes and edges (entities, claims, implicit relationships, topic clustering). (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:assemble-reviewer: Reviews the output of merge-batch-graphs.py for semantic issues the script
cannot catch. Recovers dropped nodes/edges and fills cross-batch gaps. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:domain-analyzer: Analyzes codebases to extract business domain knowledge — domains, business flows, and process steps. Produces a domain-graph.json that maps how business logic flows through the code. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:file-analyzer: Analyzes batches of source files to produce knowledge graph nodes and edges.
Extracts file structure, functions, classes, and relationships using a two-phase
approach: structural extraction script followed by LLM semantic analysis. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:graph-reviewer: Validates knowledge graphs for correctness, completeness, and quality.
Runs systematic checks and renders approval or rejection decisions. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:knowledge-graph-guide: Use this agent when users need help understanding, querying, or working
with an Understand-Anything knowledge graph. Guides users through graph
structure, node/edge relationships, layer architecture, tours, and
dashboard usage. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:project-scanner: Scans a codebase directory to produce a structured inventory of all project files,
detected languages, frameworks, import maps, and estimated complexity. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:tour-builder: Designs guided learning tours through codebases, creating 5-15 pedagogical steps
that teach project architecture and key concepts in logical order. (Tools: All tools)

You should use this skill when the user asks to create a poster, piece of art, design, or other static piece. Create original visual designs, never copying existing artists' work to avoid copyright violations.

Use this whenever the user asks an agent to ask ChatGPT, use ChatGPT Pro, compare with ChatGPT, query the ChatGPT web app, or get a second opinion specifically from their ChatGPT subscription instead of the API.

- chrome-devtools-cli: Use this skill to write shell scripts or run shell commands to automate tasks in the browser or otherwise use Chrome DevTools via CLI.
- claude-epic-pr-review: Token-intensive, maximal review of a large pull request or branch. Runs three parallel review streams — a 5-agent Codex xhigh swarm with overlapping coverage, an adversarial multi-agent epic-review workflow, and a fork that validates every existing PR comment after checks pass — then consolidates all findings, auto-fixes valid code bugs in parallel while asking the user about UX / DB-schema / new-file decisions, runs /code-review max + /simplify max, and replaces the PR. Use for large, high-risk, or cross-cutting changes when an exhaustive, deliberately expensive review is wanted.
- claude-team-review-plan-implementation: Launch a large team of agents (Codex, Opus teammates) to line-by-line compare a reference plan against its implementation across multiple repos, extract deviations, validate, fix, verify, triage design decisions with the user, simplify, and create PRs. Accepts a reference file name as its argument.
- client-forms: Create, inspect, edit, style, validate, and convert Anvil client Forms under `client_code`, including Form Python, HTML templates, event wiring, Data Bindings, RepeatingPanel item templates, reusable Forms, theme CSS, and legacy YAML templates.
- client-modules: Edit Anvil client code Python modules under `client_code` that are not form definitions, without touching read-only dependencies or form templates.
- codex-image-generation: Generate or edit images through Codex CLI's built-in image_gen tool, driven headlessly via `codex exec` on the user's ChatGPT subscription (no OPENAI_API_KEY, no browser). Use whenever the user asks an agent to "generate an image", "make an image with Codex/ChatGPT", edit an existing image, produce icons/mock-ups/hero art/social assets, or create transparent-background PNGs. Supports single generate, multi-prompt batch, image editing, and chroma-key transparency. Final images are written to `<cwd>/tmp/codex-image-generation` by default (override with `--output-dir`).
- data-models: Design idiomatic Anvil data models and client/server data flow for new apps, CRUD workflows, Data Tables, model classes, buffering, drafts, Data Bindings, and server methods. Use before choosing an architecture for persisted domain data, when the user asks about Anvil models/model classes, or when deciding whether to pass rows, model objects, dicts, or server-callable payloads.
- doc-coauthoring: Guide users through a structured workflow for co-authoring documentation. Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.

If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.

Forks (`subagent_type "fork"`, full context) do every DB sanity check, doc status update, and bug fix. Use when the user says "initiate smoke tests", "let's run the smoke tests", "start/resume smoke testing", or wants to execute a smoke-test doc against the test environment.

- mk-feature-plan-mode: Plan and prototype a feature before implementation. Reviewers iterate the plan and prototype together until the user approves the experience. Then write and open a self-contained feature_plan_<feature>.html, plus a test-verified migration.py only for non-additive schema changes. Use for "feature plan mode", "plan this feature", "design doc for ...", or any reviewable UX/architecture plan.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. - performance-metrics-from-new-relic: Use when you or the user wants frontend performance metrics from New Relic, including Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, poor distributions, and worst URLs or sessions.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. - prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- quick-smoke-tests: Generate an ordered, dependency-aware list of UI smoke tests for the work just completed in this session. Walk the user through every test using the AskUser tool — one question per test with all details embedded in the question — then validate each reported result against the database. Use when the user says "smoke test what we just did", "let's quickly verify the changes in the UI", or similar after implementation work.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud (requires claude.ai account access)); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). ## Failed runs
- Latest: run id 31860738969 — https://github.com/khairm/superset-windows-arm64/actions/runs/31860738969 — schedule, 2026-08-15 03:01 UTC, failed in 43s, target `desktop-v1.22.0`.

## Phase that failed
AI conflict resolution — the FIRST AI step, right after `git merge`. Job `merge`, step "Merge upstream + resolve + gate". Never reached MERGE-ADAPT, any gate (FEATURES.md markers, lock consistency, REFERR-GATE), the semantic review loop, the build, publish, or advance. Jobs `build` and `advance` were skipped (`- build`, `- advance in 0s`).

## Exact error
Tag detection and merge worked fine:
```
baseline=desktop-v1.20.2  latest_upstream=desktop-v1.22.0
CONFLICT (modify/delete): .github/workflows/ci.yml deleted in HEAD and modified in refs/upstream-tags/desktop-v1.22.0^{commit}...
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in AGENTS.md
```
33 conflicted files (AGENTS.md, bun.lock, apps/desktop/package.json, apps/desktop/src/main/index.ts, most of DashboardSidebar/**, 12 host-service files, packages/cli+host-service package.json, workspace-client/eventBus.ts).

```
##[group]claude resolve attempt 1
You've hit your weekly limit · resets Aug 17, 5pm (UTC)
##[group]claude resolve attempt 2
You've hit your weekly limit · resets Aug 17, 5pm (UTC)
##[group]claude resolve attempt 3

##[error]Process completed with exit code 1.
```
Byte-identical message on the Aug 14 run (for desktop-v1.21.0).

## Repair attempts
Three, all zero-work no-ops. `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\.github\workflows\nightly-merge.yml:239-245` runs `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model claude-opus-5 --effort high -p "$PROMPT" || true` in a `while [ $attempt -le 3 ]` loop with no backoff and no exit-code inspection. All three returned in under a second each; the entire loop burned 4 seconds. The `|| true` swallows the CLI failure, so the script infers "AI failed" only from surviving conflict markers — it cannot distinguish "Opus tried and lost" from "Opus never ran". That is why the annotation blames Opus for a merge it never saw.

## Root cause
Transient and external: the account behind `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` hit its **weekly** Claude usage limit, resets **Aug 17, 5pm UTC**. Not a code defect, not a bad merge, not a gate regression, not runner/network. The 33 conflicts are a normal two-version upstream delta and are unexamined — no AI ever looked at them, so we have zero evidence about whether they are hard or easy.

## State — clean, nothing to clean up
- Baseline untouched at `desktop-v1.20.2` in `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\.fork\upstream-baseline.txt`.
- No candidate branch on the remote (branches are only `main`, `entire/checkpoints/v1`, six dependabot ones). Nothing stranded.
- No Release published, no tag moved.

## Self-heal vs local fix
**Self-heals, but not before Aug 18.** Nightlies fire ~03:00 UTC; the Aug 16 and Aug 17 runs both land before the 5pm-UTC-Aug-17 reset, so expect two more identical red runs. The Aug 18 run gets quota back and merges `desktop-v1.20.2` → whatever the latest tag is then, in ONE merge — v1.21.0 is skipped entirely, not accumulated, so missed nights do not compound into multiple merges.

Caveat on that self-heal: 33 conflicted files spanning two upstream versions is a large single resolve, and every later AI phase in the same run (MERGE-ADAPT port, REFERR repair, semantic review, then BUILD-REPAIR) draws on the same token pool. A freshly-reset but heavily-used quota could abort mid-run at a later stage instead. Success on Aug 18 is likely but not assured.

**No local fix needed right now.** Specifically: do NOT act on the run's own "fix locally and re-baseline" advice — that recovery text is wrong for this failure mode and would mean hand-resolving 33 files for no reason.

## Recommended fixes
1. Do nothing urgent. Either wait for Aug 18, or after 5pm UTC Aug 17 dispatch the nightly manually rather than waiting for the schedule.
2. Classify quota/rate-limit failures separately at `.github/workflows/nightly-merge.yml:241-243`. Capture the CLI exit code and stdout instead of discarding with `|| true`; on a usage/rate-limit signature, abort with a distinct message ("AI unavailable — weekly limit, resets X — not a merge failure, retrying next night") and skip the retries. As written, every future quota outage will surface to the user as fork breakage demanding manual re-baselining. This is the one change worth making.
3. Add backoff to the retry loop — three calls in 4 seconds is not a retry strategy against any transient condition.
4. Optional: pre-flight the token's quota at job start so a limited night costs 40s and one clear annotation instead of a red run with a 33-file conflict dump.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

run_claude "resolve" "$PROMPT"; crc=$?
...
if [ $attempt -lt 3 ] && [ "$crc" -ne 0 ]; then ai_backoff "$attempt"; fi

`api error[^0-9]{0,8}(429|5[0-9][0-9])` and `(status|http)[^0-9]{0,8}(429|500|502|503|529)`.

**1. Helper lives in inline workflow YAML — repo convention says `scripts/`**
`C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\.github\workflows\nightly-merge.yml:113-207`

95 lines of step logic (classification corpus, backoff policy, abort semantics) embedded in the workflow file. AGENTS.md: "all step logic lives in `.github/actions/` + `scripts/` (repairable mid-run)" precisely because "workflow files are frozen once a run starts."

Cost: `AI_HARD_RE`/`AI_SOFT_RE` are a *drifting heuristic corpus* — new Anthropic wording is the expected failure mode, not the exception. In YAML, a miss can't be fixed for the running night and can't be fixed by any repair agent; it's next-run-only. It also can't be unit-tested and can't be called from anywhere else (see #2).

Re your note on frozen gate scripts: that freeze is a per-file allowlist inside `scripts/ci-repair.sh:134`'s prompt, not an argument against `scripts/` hosting. Script-hosting gives the maintainer the *choice* to freeze; YAML-hosting forecloses it.

Deeper: `scripts/ai-run.sh` sourced by the workflow step.

---

**2. Second copy of the same problem in `ci-repair.sh` doesn't get the fix**
`C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\scripts\ci-repair.sh:143-150` and `:184-189`

`(BUILD-REPAIR)`'s agent step runs `claude` bare → captures rc → emits `::warning::`; push step re-derives a coarse "rc≠0 + untouched tree = AI infra failure." Same OAuth token, same account, same night — a weekly cap that kills the merge AI kills the build AI too. No HARD/SOFT split, no backoff, no retry: quota exhaustion burns both repair rounds in seconds and reports `agent made no changes and did not declare retry-only — cannot repair. Failing loud` — the exact false verdict this diff exists to kill, one job over.

Cost: fix is half-applied. Wrapper defined inline in the YAML step is unreachable from `ci-repair.sh`; completing it means copy-pasting 95 lines, after which the two regex corpora drift independently.

Deeper: `scripts/ai-run.sh` sourced by both. `ci-repair.sh`'s `$STATE_DIR/claude-rc` becomes `claude-rc` + `claude-verdict` (`AI_UNAVAILABLE`/`RAN`) so the push step *reads* a classification instead of guessing one from tree state.

---

**3. Classification corpus is a hand-translated, untested copy of a tested TS classifier**
`nightly-merge.yml:143-144` vs `apps\desktop\src\main\lib\auto-resume\classifier\classifier.ts:61-92` (`AUTH_TEXT`/`POLICY_TEXT`/`TRANSIENT_TEXT`/`CONN_TEXT`/`SERVER_STATUS`) — which ships `classifier.test.ts` next to it.

The comment is honest that it mirrors that file — but mirroring is the problem, not the mitigation. TS side is substring arrays with tests; YAML side is one hand-fused ERE with none. Update one, the other rots silently, and the rot only surfaces on a night the AI is down — the one night nobody is watching.

Cost: two sources of truth for "is this Anthropic infra or model prose," one covered by tests and one uncoverable by construction.

Deeper: single corpus, one consumer each side. `scripts/classify-ai-failure.mjs <logfile>` printing `HARD|SOFT|NONE`, reading a dependency-free shared corpus that `classifier.ts` also imports; `classifier.test.ts` patterns then cover the CI path. Wrapper shrinks to ~15 lines. Collapses #1, #2, #3 into one design. (`setup-node@v4` runs before every call site, so `node` is available — no bootstrap problem.)

---

**4. `die_ai_unavailable` hardcodes 2 `::endgroup::`; 3 of 5 call sites are depth 1**
`nightly-merge.yml:146-154`

Measured depths: `resolve` (337) = 1, `merge-adapt-port` (373) = 1, `merge-adapt-round` (621) = 1, `referr-repair` (463+490) = 2, `review` (568+576) = 2. Constant is right for two sites, one too many for three.

Cost: today cosmetic only (a stray `::endgroup::` with no open group is ignored). The real cost is the coupling: the constant's correctness rests on a manual audit of group nesting that nothing re-runs. Add a wrapping group anywhere in this 550-line script and the fatal error renders *inside a collapsed group* — the exact failure the function exists to prevent, and silent.

Deeper, preferred: invert the coupling — `run_claude` returns a distinguished code (e.g. 78) for AI-unavailable, call sites `::endgroup::` their own groups then call `die_ai_unavailable`. Helper stops knowing about call-site structure at all.
Deeper, cheaper: generalize instead of special-casing the deepest site — `open_group`/`close_group` wrappers maintaining `GROUP_DEPTH`; `die_ai_unavailable` emits exactly `$GROUP_DEPTH`. No call-site restructuring, magic number becomes derived.

---

**5. Retry/backoff now owned by two layers that mean different things**
`nightly-merge.yml:341, 494, 580` (new outer `ai_backoff`) vs `:196-205` (inner)

Inner retry = "CLI never reached the model" (transient API). Outer retry = "model ran, didn't finish the job." Different conditions, now sharing one knob. The three new outer `ai_backoff` calls fire on paths where the inner layer already returned — either rc=0 (model ran fine, left conflicts) or an unclassified nonzero swallowed by `|| true`. Neither has a transient condition to wait out; the sleep is cargo-cult.

Cost: retry budget became a product, not a sum. Resolve site worst case = 3 outer × 3 inner = 9 CLI invocations + 450s of pure sleeping, on the job's long pole. Nobody can state worst-case wall clock without multiplying.

Deeper: backoff belongs solely to `run_claude` — the only layer that knows *why* it's waiting. Drop the three outer `ai_backoff` calls. If outer pacing is separately wanted, that's a non-AI concern and should be named as one rather than borrowing this fix's vocabulary.

---

**Not findings:** 35-line rationale comment block is idiomatic for this file. Per-round labels (`review-round-$round`) correctly avoid log clobbering. `errexit` save/restore in `run_claude` is correct.</result>

1	<!-- ===================================================================== -->
2	<!-- FORK MAINTENANCE (khairm Windows ARM64 fork). Everything ABOVE the -->
3	<!-- divider is about maintaining this fork; everything BELOW is upstream  -->
4	<!-- superset's own developer guide, unchanged, for working on the app.    -->
5	<!-- ===================================================================== -->
6	
7	# superset-windows-arm64 — Windows ARM64 fork maintenance
8	
9	This repo is a **vendored fork** of [superset-sh/superset]: the full upstream
10	source with our Windows ARM64 + feature changes committed on top, plus CI that
11	builds a native **Windows ARM64** one-click NSIS installer. The fork is the
12	source of truth; we track upstream by **merging its deltas**, not by
13	re-applying changes. `.fork/upstream-baseline.txt` records the upstream
14	`desktop-v*` tag the baseline currently sits on.
15	
16	## Setup / architecture (high level)
17	
18	- **Build (deterministic steps, self-repairing).** `.github/workflows/build-arm64.yml`
19	  orchestrates a bounded attempt/repair loop `(BUILD-REPAIR)`: the actual build
20	  steps (install → compile → materialize the win-arm64 native closure
21	  (`scripts/materialize-native-closure.sh`: libsql/tokenizers/node-pty) →
22	  package the installer → verify packaged natives are ARM64 → publish) live in
23	  `.github/actions/arm64-build/action.yml` as thin shims over `scripts/*.sh`.
24	  A failed attempt triggers an Opus 5 (`claude-opus-5`, effort high) repair job
25	  that reads the failed log, fixes the checked-out tree, and pushes to the
26	  repair branch (nightly candidate / dispatched branch); the next attempt
27	  builds that exact sha so every deterministic gate re-runs. Max 3 attempts /
28	  2 repairs, then fail loud. Repairs may never change the app version or touch
29	  `FEATURES.md` (`scripts/check-feature-markers.mjs` gates marker survival).
30	- **Nightly merge.** `.github/workflows/nightly-merge.yml` (02:13 UTC): when
31	  upstream publishes a newer `desktop-v*` tag, git merges it; Opus 5 resolves
32	  conflicted files, then a `(MERGE-ADAPT)` proactive port pass adapts fork-only
33	  callers to cleanly-merging upstream API refactors. Deterministic gates follow
34	  (FEATURES.md marker survival, dependency/lock consistency, `(REFERR-GATE)`
35	  cannot-find-name check), then a bounded `(MERGE-SEMANTIC-GATE)` review →
36	  adapt → fresh-review loop (max 3 reviews / 2 repairs). Green all the way =
37	  build (with its own repair loop), publish the Release, advance the baseline
38	  to the BUILT sha; ANY unrepaired failure hard-aborts with the baseline
39	  untouched → fix locally with the maintainer and re-baseline. A
40	  `rehearse=true` dispatch replays a night's merge half with zero side effects.
41	- **Key files.** `FEATURES.md` (feature manifest + fenced `markers` block the
42	  gates parse), `.fork/upstream-baseline.txt`,
43	  `scripts/check-dangerous-diagnostics.mjs` (REFERR gate),
44	  `scripts/check-feature-markers.mjs` (standalone marker gate),
45	  `scripts/ci-repair.sh` (build-repair engine),
46	  `scripts/ai-run.sh` ((AI-UNAVAILABLE) classification + shared Claude CLI wrapper),
47	  `scripts/check-override-consistency.mjs`, `scripts/resolve-release-age.mjs`,
48	  companion native packages `github.com/khairm/libsql-windows-arm64` +
49	  `github.com/khairm/tokenizers-windows-arm64`.
50	
51	## Non-negotiables
52	
53	- **Whole feature set or fail loud** — every `FEATURES.md` marker survives a
54	  merge or the run aborts; never ship a partial fork.
55	- **v2-only, forever** — the v2 cloud/host-service stack is pinned on; never v1.
56	- **One version, ever** — exactly one Release per upstream version, tagged
57	  `desktop-v<version>`, rebuilt in place; no betas/prereleases.
58	- **No build-time type/test gate except `(REFERR-GATE)`** — the tree carries
59	  accepted type debt; only cannot-find-name diagnostics fail the build.
60	  Validate + e2e locally before relying on a release.
61	- **Everything is AI-touchable** (needs `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`): the nightly
62	  merge resolves/ports/reviews, and the build self-repairs via `(BUILD-REPAIR)`.
63	  Workflow YAML self-repair additionally needs the `WORKFLOW_PUSH_TOKEN` secret
64	  (fine-grained PAT, Contents+Workflows write) and only takes effect the NEXT
65	  run — workflow files are frozen once a run starts, which is why all step
66	  logic lives in `.github/actions/` + `scripts/` (repairable mid-run).
67	  Rate-limited/unparsable AI output aborts rather than ships.
68	
69	## Custom features / overrides
70	
71	`FEATURES.md` is the authoritative manifest (descriptions + marker tokens).
72	In brief:
73	
74	- **Native Windows ARM64 packaging** — one-click installer; ARM64 node-pty,
75	  libsql, tokenizers; renderer CORS for `superset-app://`.
76	- **Window controls** — native `titleBarOverlay` is the sole min/max/close on
77	  Windows, theme-matched; upstream's duplicates hidden.
78	- **Windows behaviour fixes** — skip quit-confirm; cmd.exe fallback;
79	  force-foreground; hidden-window watchdog; WebGL first-paint recovery; Wispr
80	  Flow accessibility/paste fix; fast non-blocking startup.
81	- **Agent status dots (Claude + Codex)** — per-terminal + workspace-rollup dot:
82	  red = needs input, yellow = working (incl. subagents/teammates/compaction/
83	  codex-companion holds), green = ready for review, blue = shell/background/
84	  cloud activity; precedence red > yellow > blue > green. All surfaces (tab,
85	  pane header, sidebar row + agent chips, rollup, kanban card) derive from one
86	  per-source primitive with independent latched axes; hook-driven via
87	  `superset-notify.py` POSTs with self-healing markers and persistence across
88	  renderer reloads; companion phone/watch alerts cover blocked questions,
89	  ready-for-review, and terminal-agent failures.
90	- **Auto-resume** — after an API failure, idle Claude terminals re-send
91	  automatically (bounded retries/budget, default-on, away-detection).
92	- **Recycle Bin** — every delete entry point soft-deletes (30-day display
93	  window); permanent delete only from inside the bin.
94	- **Non-git / multi-repo workspaces** — open any folder (non-git or multi-repo)
95	  as a plain workspace.
96	- **Multi-repo branch workspaces** — group N git repos under one project row;
97	  its "+" fans a branch out as worktrees per member (all-or-nothing, adoption
98	  on resume, editable membership, loud partial-state failures).
99	- **Workspace branch label** — branch name top-right in the tab bar; click
100	  copies.
101	- **Thread snooze / archive** — timed Snooze (auto-returns) + sticky Archive in
102	  revealable sidebar sections.
103	- **Sidebar** — pinned > active > idle tier sort with stable manual drag order;
104	  hover freezes re-sorting.
105	- **Terminal links** — plain click copies a URL/path; Ctrl/Cmd+click opens.
106	- **Agent-hook bash-wrap** — Gemini/Cursor `.sh` hooks run via Git-for-Windows
107	  bash.
108	- **Kanban board** — device-local board of every sidebar project's branches +
109	  Queued and final Completed columns, custom columns, deadlines, per-column
110	  date filters, promote-to-branch drag, sidebar Mark completed for active
111	  worktrees, frozen completed records, append-only daily JSON backups under
112	  `~/.superset/backups/kanban/`.
113	
114	## Live footguns (do NOT repeat)
115	
116	- No synchronous/blocking fs on the main thread at startup — the renderer's
117	  `superset-app://` loader starves and the window stays blank for minutes.
118	- Never re-enable xterm `screenReaderMode` (Wispr Flow regression); the build
119	  hard-fails if it is truthy in a renderer bundle.
120	- Never let `ws` load native bufferutil/utf-8-validate in the host-service —
121	  keep `WS_NO_BUFFER_UTIL=1` + `WS_NO_UTF_8_VALIDATE=1` in the coordinator
122	  child env AND first-import in serve.ts.
123	- Keep agent-hook `.sh` templates pipeline-free (bash builtins only) —
124	  subprocess-fork cascades crash emulated msys2 on ARM64 (`(HOOK-FORK-DIET)`).
125	- `.github/workflows` is fork-owned and CI's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can never push

Read `git diff HEAD` (4 files) + `scripts/ai-run.sh` in full, plus `ci-repair.sh` whole, `build-arm64.yml` job wiring, `check-feature-markers.mjs`, and every `run_claude` call site.

Overall altitude: extraction itself is right. One shared wrapper, one raw `claude` invocation left in the repo (`scripts/ai-run.sh:113`), one `npm install -g` (`:95`), all merge call sites plain (no subshell/pipeline → `exit 99` propagates correctly). Findings below are round-2 residue, not the core design.

## 1. Mechanism generalized, invariant not gated — `FEATURES.md:151` + `nightly-merge.yml:113`
Marker row `(AI-UNAVAILABLE)\t.github/workflows` is satisfied by exactly one token in that tree: a **comment** (`# --- (AI-UNAVAILABLE) shared Claude CLI wrapper ---`, line 113). Load-bearing line is `source scripts/ai-run.sh` (line 119), unmarked.
Cost: the two failure modes invert. Reformat/merge drops the comment → gate fails though the wrapper is intact. Conversely an upstream merge or edit deletes `source …` / re-adds `claude … || true` → comment survives, gate green, protection silently gone — the exact 2026-08-13/14 regression class this change exists to prevent.
Deeper: drop the `.github/workflows` row (mechanism lives in `scripts/ai-run.sh`, already covered by its own row) and assert the real invariant instead — a one-line gate: no `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` outside `scripts/ai-run.sh`. Matches AGENTS.md's own "assert the invariant over the whole artifact set" footgun.

## 2. Verdict protocol carries one fact in two files — `ci-repair.sh:160,174,177,203,222`
`claude-verdict` (string `AI_UNAVAILABLE`|`RAN`) and `claude-rc` (number) both record "did the AI run", read at two places with two different `|| echo unknown` fallbacks, and the literal `"AI_UNAVAILABLE"` is hard-coded once in `agent` mode and again in `push` mode — unconnected to `AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT=99` sourced right there.
Cost: three states now representable (verdict/rc agree, disagree, absent) for two real ones; `claude-rc` is deliberately never written on the unavailable path, so line 222's fallback is dead for that case and future readers can't tell whether that's intent or a hole.
Deeper: one file. Write `$AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT` into `claude-rc` pessimistically before the call, overwrite with the real rc after, and have `push` compare numerically against the sourced constant. Same pessimism, one channel, no duplicated literal.

## 3. Env-var config sprawl + unvalidated boundary — `ai-run.sh:59-60,75`; `ci-repair.sh:33-41`
Three independently-settable knobs, all `${VAR:-default}`, two of which exist only to compose one sentence. `AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT` (55) is a hard assignment — no stated rule for which constants are overridable.
Concrete costs:
- `${:-}` makes safety policy readable from the **ambient CI environment**, not just the consumer. `ci-repair.sh` hard-assigns (safe); `nightly-merge.yml` sets none, so a stray `AI_RUN_MAX_TRIES` in workflow/action env silently changes the merge's retry budget. `.github/actions/**` is not in `FROZEN_GATE_PATHS`.
- Nothing enforces coherence of the triple — `AI_RUN_CONTEXT="merge"` with build-repair recovery prose is representable and would print a wrong recovery instruction on the one path whose whole job is telling the operator what to do.
- `AI_RUN_MAX_TRIES` is never validated as numeric ≥1. `seq 1 0` (or a non-numeric value) yields an empty loop → `run_claude` falls off the `for` at line 154 and **returns 0**. Caller records `RAN`, rc=0, untouched tree → "agent made no changes — cannot repair", i.e. a false verdict about the build, precisely the bug class this file exists to kill. Violates the repo's "validate at API boundaries" rule.
Deeper: one key, `AI_RUN_CONTEXT=merge|build-repair`, resolved inside `ai-run.sh` to a `(recovery text, max tries)` pair; hard assignment, not `:-`; `case` on unknown context → die; add explicit `return 1` after the loop so the function can never fall through as success.

## 4. `AI_RUN_MAX_TRIES` conflates count with policy — `ai-run.sh:75,151`
The same number governs "how many transient retries" and "when a soft signature escalates to a hard abort". `=1` means "never retry" *and* "any transient → AI-UNAVAILABLE" — correct behaviour, but expressed as an off-label retry counter needing 6 lines of comment to decode.
Cost: policy intent is unreadable from the call site; a future tweak to the retry budget silently moves the escalation threshold too.
Deeper: name the policy (`AI_RUN_ON_TRANSIENT=retry|abort`) and let the count follow, or fold both into the context table from #3.

## 5. Exit-99 → return-code conversion done ad hoc per call site — `ci-repair.sh:168`
`( ensure_claude && run_claude … ) || CLAUDE_RC=$?`. The abort/catch decision is a subshell trick at the call site rather than a stance declared by the consumer.
Cost: (a) a second AI call in build-repair needs its own subshell and its own re-check of `AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT`; (b) the subshell permanently forecloses `run_claude` returning state to its caller (log path, matched signature, classification) — anything richer than an int has to leave via a file; (c) the same function has abort-vs-catch semantics depending on invisible call-site shape, which currently holds only because all five merge call sites happen to be plain commands.
Deeper: opt-in in `ai-run.sh` — `AI_RUN_ON_UNAVAILABLE=abort|return`; in `return` mode `die_ai_unavailable` prints, sets `AI_RUN_UNAVAILABLE=1`, and returns `$AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT`. One line at the top of `ci-repair.sh`, no subshell, no per-call-site knowledge.

## 6. Minor
- `ai-run.sh:110` `${RUNNER_TEMP:?}` + `::error::` output make a `scripts/`-hosted "shared" library GH-Actions-only. `AI_RUN_LOG_DIR="${RUNNER_TEMP:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}}"` costs one line and makes local rehearsal possible.
- Two resolution styles for one dependency: relative `source scripts/ai-run.sh` (`nightly-merge.yml:119`, cwd-dependent) vs `$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/ai-run.sh` (`ci-repair.sh:43`). Pick one.

Deeper: drop the `.github/workflows` row (mechanism lives in `scripts/ai-run.sh`, already covered by its own row) and assert the real invariant instead — a one-line gate: no `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` outside `scripts/ai-run.sh`. ## 2. Verdict protocol carries one fact in two files — `ci-repair.sh:160,174,177,203,222`
`claude-verdict` (string `AI_UNAVAILABLE`|`RAN`) and `claude-rc` (number) both record "did the AI run", read at two places with two different `|| echo unknown` fallbacks, and the literal `"AI_UNAVAILABLE"` is hard-coded once in `agent` mode and again in `push` mode — unconnected to `AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT=99` sourced right there.

## 3. Env-var config sprawl + unvalidated boundary — `ai-run.sh:59-60,75`; `ci-repair.sh:33-41`
Three independently-settable knobs, all `${VAR:-default}`, two of which exist only to compose one sentence. `AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT` (55) is a hard assignment — no stated rule for which constants are overridable.
Concrete costs:
- `${:-}` makes safety policy readable from the **ambient CI environment**, not just the consumer. `ci-repair.sh` hard-assigns (safe); `nightly-merge.yml` sets none, so a stray `AI_RUN_MAX_TRIES` in workflow/action env silently changes the merge's retry budget. `.github/actions/**` is not in `FROZEN_GATE_PATHS`.
- Nothing enforces coherence of the triple — `AI_RUN_CONTEXT="merge"` with build-repair recovery prose is representable and would print a wrong recovery instruction on the one path whose whole job is telling the operator what to do.

Cost: policy intent is unreadable from the call site; a future tweak to the retry budget silently moves the escalation threshold too.
Deeper: name the policy (`AI_RUN_ON_TRANSIENT=retry|abort`) and let the count follow, or fold both into the context table from #3.

Deeper: opt-in in `ai-run.sh` — `AI_RUN_ON_UNAVAILABLE=abort|return`; in `return` mode `die_ai_unavailable` prints, sets `AI_RUN_UNAVAILABLE=1`, and returns `$AI_UNAVAILABLE_EXIT`. One line at the top of `ci-repair.sh`, no subshell, no per-call-site knowledge.

## 6. Minor
- `ai-run.sh:110` `${RUNNER_TEMP:?}` + `::error::` output make a `scripts/`-hosted "shared" library GH-Actions-only. `AI_RUN_LOG_DIR="${RUNNER_TEMP:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}}"` costs one line and makes local rehearsal possible.

- `ci-repair.sh:43` sources at top level, so `collect` and `push` load the wrapper they never use; `push` then compares a string literal instead of the constant it just sourced (see #2).

No findings on the deliberate decisions listed as out of scope. Nothing edited.</result>
